Senses.Explanation: Literally, the king of elephants. Chan records repeatedly take the elephant king's bearing, stride, and backward look as publicly recognizable forms of a master's conduct. One master looks right and says, 'the bearing of the elephant king—how could it forget the backward look?' Another stock pairing says, 'in the lion's den there is no other beast; where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease.' The backward look itself enters encounter history: when a teacher mounts the seat and says 'the lion frowns; the elephant king looks back,' a monk awakens, enters the room, and presents his understanding. Later verse calls the lion's vigorous motion world-shaking and the elephant king's backward look effortless. The line can also be tested rather than merely praised: when a monk quotes 'where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease,' the master drives him out with blows. The Chan-specific bend is this deployment of a royal animal's gait and backward glance as teaching-seat bearing and encounter language. The records assign no further gloss to the image, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 809 hits in 242 texts. Family check covered the elephant king's stride (象王行), backward look or turn (象王回顧／回旋), the lion's roar or vigorous motion (師子吼／奮迅), the fragrant elephant (香象), and Samantabhadra's (普賢) white elephant. The primary Chan image and the Buddhist narrative animal share the same royal-elephant referent, so differing deployments were not split into readings. The narrative white-elephant witness remains listed in SourceTexts but was not curated because it adds outside-story identity rather than defining the Chan bend.

Occurrences.Kwic: 顧右邊曰：象王之儀，寧忘回顧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷). Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), Changlu Timing section. Changlu Timing is the exact hall speaker who looks to his right and says that the deportment of the elephant king does not forget to look back.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師子窟中無異獸。象王行處絕狐蹤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Meeting the Source (五燈會元), Luopu Yuanan section. Luopu Yuanan is the exact speaker answering whether patriarchal intent and scriptural intent are the same or different: no other beast inhabits the lion's den, and fox tracks cease where the elephant king walks.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遠禪師陞堂，顧視大眾云：師子嚬呻，象王回顧。師忽有省，入室陳解。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Jianzhong Jingguo Continuation of the Lamp Record (建中靖國續燈錄), in Kaixian Shanxian's biography. Fushan Fayuan, named 遠禪師 in the case, is the exact speaker of 師子嚬呻，象王回顧; Kaixian hears it, awakens, and enters the room to present his understanding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧云：「象王行處絕狐蹤。」師直打退
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan (隱元禪師語錄), Yinyuan Longqi's Huangbo Mountain record. An unnamed monk is the exact speaker of 'where the elephant king walks, fox tracks vanish'; Yinyuan Longqi immediately drives him back with blows. The line, expanded context, section header, book title, TEI header, and corpus parallels do not name this monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師子奮迅𠔃搖蕩乾坤象王回𣒀兮不費餘力
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 禪宗頌古聯珠通集, verse on the Woman Emerging from Samadhi case. Yuanwu Keqin is the exact verse author: the source's inline attribution at the end of this individual verse is 圓悟勤, and the stored elephant-king line is inside that verse.
